da-2026-2-da-1.approach: Read $C$ off the soft-margin objective $\frac12\lVert w\rVert^2 + C\sum_i \xi_i$: $C$ is the price of each slack, so $C\to\infty$ forbids slack and the problem becomes the hard-margin SVM.

steps.title: Soft-margin primal
steps.body:
$$\min_{w,b,\xi}\; \tfrac12\lVert w\rVert^2 + C\sum_{i=1}^{n}\xi_i \quad \text{s.t. } y_i(w^\top x_i+b)\ge 1-\xi_i,\; \xi_i\ge 0$$
The first term rewards a wide margin ($\text{margin} = 2/\lVert w\rVert$); the second penalises each margin violation $\xi_i>0$ at rate $C$.

steps.title: Let $C\to\infty$
steps.body: Any $\xi_i>0$ costs an unbounded amount, so the optimum sets every $\xi_i = 0$: all points must satisfy $y_i(w^\top x_i+b)\ge1$. This is exactly the **hard-margin** SVM (in the dual, the box $0\le\alpha_i\le C$ becomes $\alpha_i\ge0$).

steps.title: Consequence
steps.body: The boundary bends to classify every training point (including noise/outliers) correctly with margin, typically giving a **narrower margin and high variance — overfitting**. (Small $C$ is the opposite: wide margin, many violations, risk of underfitting.)

answer.value: Option **(A)** — hard margin, zero violations, overfitting risk

optionAnalysis.reason: Infinite slack penalty forces $\xi_i = 0$ — the hard-margin SVM, which overfits noisy data.
Describes $C\to 0$: violations become free, so only the margin term matters.
Large $C$ drives slacks to zero, not up; excessive slack/underfitting is the small-$C$ regime.
The problem stays a constrained QP (hard-margin); it is not turned into least-squares regression (that is LS-SVM, a different formulation).

da-2026-2-da-1.shortcut: $C$ multiplies the error term: large $C$ ⇒ 'make no training errors' ⇒ hard margin ⇒ low bias, high variance.
pitfalls: Mixing up $C$ with the $\lambda$ of ridge/lasso: in SVM a **large** $C$ means **weak** regularisation (as $C \propto 1/\lambda$).
da-2026-2-da-1.verification: Equivalent form $\min \lambda\lVert w\rVert^2 + \sum_i \max(0, 1-y_if(x_i))$ with $\lambda = \frac1{2C}$: $C\to\infty$ ⇒ $\lambda\to0$ ⇒ no regularisation ⇒ overfitting.

da-2026-2-da-2.approach: Look at each activation's gradient for negative inputs: 'dying' happens only when that gradient is exactly zero, so a unit stuck in the negative region never receives an update.

steps.title: Mechanism of a dead unit
steps.body: If a unit's pre-activation $z = w^\top x + b$ is negative for every training input, its output is $f(z)$ and the gradient reaching $w, b$ is $f'(z)\cdot(\dots)$. If $f'(z) = 0$ for all $z<0$, then $w, b$ never change again — the unit is permanently dead.

steps.title: Negative-side gradient of each option
steps.body:
| Activation | $f(z)$, $z<0$ | $f'(z)$, $z<0$ |
|---|---|---|
| ReLU | $0$ | $0$ |
| Leaky ReLU | $0.01z$ | $0.01$ |
| ELU | $\alpha(e^z-1)$ | $\alpha e^z>0$ |
| GELU | $z\,\Phi(z)$ | $\Phi(z)+z\varphi(z)$, nonzero almost everywhere |

steps.title: Conclude
steps.body: Only **ReLU** has an identically zero gradient on the whole negative half-line, so only it suffers from dying units. Leaky ReLU, ELU and GELU were introduced partly to fix this.

optionAnalysis.reason: $f'(z) = 0$ for all $z<0$: a unit pushed into the negative region gets no gradient and never recovers.
Leaky ReLU keeps slope $0.01$ for $z<0$ — designed specifically to prevent dying ReLU.
ELU's negative-side gradient $\alpha e^z$ is positive, so the unit can still learn.
GELU is smooth with a nonzero gradient for negative inputs (except one isolated point), so units do not die.

pitfalls: Confusing dying ReLU (exactly zero gradient) with vanishing gradients of sigmoid/tanh (small but nonzero).
da-2026-2-da-2.verification: Common causes of dead ReLUs — a large learning rate or a strongly negative bias — push $z<0$ for all inputs; with Leaky ReLU the $0.01$ slope still pulls the bias back up.

da-2026-2-da-5.approach: Worst case for separate chaining is the adversarial input where every key hashes to the same slot: the table degenerates into one linked list of length $n$, and an (unsuccessful) search scans all of it.

steps.title: How a search works with chaining
steps.body: Search for key $k$: compute $h(k)$ in $O(1)$, then walk the linked list (chain) stored in slot $h(k)$, comparing $k$ with each element. Cost $= O(1) + O(\text{length of that chain})$.

steps.title: Worst case: all keys collide
steps.body: Nothing stops all $n$ keys from hashing to the same slot (e.g. a poor hash function or adversarial keys). Then one chain holds all $n$ elements, and the other $m-1$ slots are empty.

scene.caption: Searching for an absent key compares it with all $n$ nodes.

steps.title: Cost of the search
steps.body: Searching for a key that is absent (or at the tail) compares it with all $n$ elements of that chain: $\Theta(1) + \Theta(n) = \Theta(n)$. The table size $m$ does not matter here.

steps.title: Contrast with the average case
steps.body: Under simple uniform hashing the expected chain length is the load factor $\alpha = n/m$, giving $\Theta(1 + \alpha)$ on average — which is $\Theta(1)$ only when $n = O(m)$. The question asks for the **worst** case: $\Theta(n)$.

This is the *average* case with a constant load factor ($\Theta(1+\alpha)$, $\alpha = O(1)$), not the worst case.
Logarithmic time would need a balanced search tree in each bucket; plain chaining uses linked lists.
The chain length depends on $n$, not on the table size $m$; even scanning every slot is not the cost of one chained search.

da-2026-2-da-6.approach: With a closed list, A* never re-expands a node, so the first time a node is expanded its $g$ must already be optimal. Consistency ($h(n) \le c(n,n') + h(n')$) guarantees exactly that; admissibility alone does not, as a 5-node counterexample shows.
concepts: Graph search with a closed list

steps.title: The two properties
steps.body:
- **Admissible:** $h(n) \le h^*(n)$ (never overestimates the true cost to the goal).
- **Consistent:** $h(n) \le c(n,n') + h(n')$ for every edge $n \to n'$, and $h(\text{goal}) = 0$. Consistent ⇒ admissible, not conversely.

steps.title: Why consistency suffices
steps.body: If $h$ is consistent, then along any path $f(n') = g(n) + c(n,n') + h(n') \ge g(n) + h(n) = f(n)$: $f$ never decreases. Hence A* expands nodes in non-decreasing $f$ order, and when a node is first expanded (and moved to the closed list) it has been reached by an optimal path. Never reopening it is therefore safe, and the goal is returned with optimal cost.

steps.title: Admissible-only counterexample: setup

steps.title: What a moving average needs
steps.body: For each row (e.g. each day of each store) we want the average of that row and its previous few rows **in the same group, in time order**, while keeping one output row per input row. GROUP BY cannot do this — it collapses each group to a single row.

steps.title: The window clause
steps.body:
A window function attaches an aggregate to every row:

```sql
SELECT store, day, sales,
       AVG(sales) OVER (PARTITION BY store
                        ORDER BY day
                        ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS ma3
FROM daily_sales;
```

steps.title: Ridge objective
steps.body:
Ridge regression minimises the residual sum of squares plus an L2 penalty:
$$J(w) = \sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(y_i - x_i^\top w\right)^2 + \lambda\sum_{j=1}^{p} w_j^2,\qquad \lambda \ge 0.$$
The penalty is $\lambda\lVert w\rVert_2^2$ — the **sum of squared weights** (the intercept is usually not penalised).

steps.body:
Setting $\nabla J = -2X^\top(y - Xw) + 2\lambda w = 0$ gives
$$\hat w_{\text{ridge}} = (X^\top X + \lambda I)^{-1}X^\top y.$$
With orthonormal features ($X^\top X = I$) this is $\hat w_{\text{ridge}} = \dfrac{\hat w_{\text{OLS}}}{1+\lambda}$: every coefficient is scaled down by the factor $\frac{1}{1+\lambda}$, smoothly towards $0$ but never exactly to $0$.

steps.body: The penalised quantity is $\sum_j w_j^2$ → option **(A)**. $\sum_j |w_j|$ is the lasso (L1) penalty, and rank / condition number are not penalty terms at all.
